title: KS3 / Year 7-9 Science - Biology: Organisation
description: Reading comprehension pack covering organisation, digestion, enzymes, food tests, gas exchange and practical interpretation for KS3 biology.
subtitle: Reading passages for KS3 Biology: Organisation.

data.sourcePassage: Large multicellular organisms are organised in levels. A cell is the smallest living unit. Some cells become specialised, which means they have adaptations for particular jobs. Similar specialised cells work together as tissues. Different tissues combine to form organs, and organs work together in organ systems. For example, the stomach is an organ because it contains muscle tissue, glandular tissue, epithelial tissue, nervous tissue and blood tissue. These tissues work together to store food, churn it, produce digestive juices, protect the stomach lining and transport substances. The full sequence is cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism. This organisation matters because a large organism cannot rely on every cell doing every job independently.

questions.question: Explain why specialised cells are useful in multicellular organisms.
questions.modelAnswer: Specialised cells have adaptations for particular jobs, so the organism can carry out many functions efficiently.

data.sourcePassage: Digestion is the breakdown of large insoluble food molecules into smaller soluble molecules. Food passes through the mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum and anus. It does not pass through the liver, gall bladder or pancreas, although these organs help digestion by adding substances. In the mouth, chewing breaks food into smaller pieces and saliva begins starch digestion. In the stomach, food is churned and protease begins protein digestion. In the small intestine, digestion is completed and digested nutrients are absorbed into the blood. Villi in the small intestine increase surface area and have thin walls and a good blood supply. Undigested material moves to the large intestine, where water is absorbed, then faeces are stored in the rectum and removed by egestion.

questions.question: Name the tube that carries food from the mouth to the stomach.
questions.modelAnswer: The oesophagus carries food from the mouth to the stomach.

questions.question: Where does most absorption of digested nutrients happen?
questions.modelAnswer: Most absorption happens in the small intestine.

questions.question: Why do villi make absorption more efficient?
questions.modelAnswer: Villi increase surface area and have thin walls and a good blood supply, so nutrients can move into blood quickly.

questions.question: Explain why food does not need to pass through the pancreas for the pancreas to help digestion.
questions.modelAnswer: The pancreas releases digestive enzymes into the digestive system, so it can help chemical digestion without food passing through it.

questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes digestion from absorption?
questions.modelAnswer: Digestion breaks food down, while absorption moves digested nutrients into blood.
options: Digestion is movement of nutrients into blood; absorption is breakdown of food.
Digestion is breakdown of food; absorption is movement of digested nutrients into blood.
Both words mean removal of faeces.

data.sourcePassage: Enzymes are biological catalysts. They speed up reactions without being used up. Digestive enzymes are specific: amylase breaks starch into sugars, protease breaks proteins into amino acids, and lipase breaks lipids into fatty acids and glycerol. Enzymes have optimum conditions. If the temperature is too high, an enzyme may denature, changing shape so the substrate no longer fits well. Bile is made by the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It is not an enzyme, but it helps lipid digestion by emulsifying fats into tiny droplets. Food tests identify particular nutrients. Iodine turns blue-black if starch is present. Benedict's solution turns green, yellow, orange or brick-red after warming if reducing sugar is present. Biuret reagent turns lilac or purple for protein, and the ethanol emulsion test gives a cloudy white emulsion for lipids.

data.sourcePassage: Breathing, gas exchange and respiration are different processes. Breathing, or ventilation, moves air into and out of the lungs. During inhalation, the intercostal muscles contract, the ribs move up and out, and the diaphragm contracts and flattens. Chest volume increases, pressure decreases, and air moves in. During exhalation, the muscles relax, chest volume decreases, pressure increases, and air moves out. Gas exchange happens in the alveoli. Oxygen diffuses from the air in the alveoli into the blood, while carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli. Alveoli are adapted with a large surface area, thin walls, moist surfaces, good blood supply and ventilation. Respiration is a chemical reaction inside cells that releases energy from glucose. Aerobic respiration uses glucose and oxygen and produces carbon dioxide and water.

questions.question: Where does gas exchange happen in the lungs?
questions.modelAnswer: Gas exchange happens in the alveoli.

questions.question: What happens to the diaphragm during inhalation?
questions.modelAnswer: During inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and flattens.
options: It turns oxygen into carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Explain why oxygen diffuses from alveoli into the blood.
questions.modelAnswer: Oxygen concentration is higher in the alveoli than in the blood arriving at the lungs, so oxygen moves down its concentration gradient into blood.

questions.question: Why is breathing not the same as respiration?
questions.modelAnswer: Breathing moves air into and out of the lungs, while respiration is a chemical reaction inside cells that releases energy.

questions.question: Which adaptation keeps the concentration gradient for gas exchange steep?
questions.modelAnswer: Ventilation keeps fresh air reaching alveoli, helping maintain a steep concentration gradient.
options: ventilation bringing fresh air to alveoli

data.sourcePassage: A common KS3 practical investigates how temperature affects amylase activity. Amylase breaks starch into sugars, and iodine can show whether starch is still present. Iodine turns blue-black when starch is present and stays brown or orange when starch has disappeared. In the method, starch, buffer and amylase are warmed to the chosen temperature. The amylase and starch are mixed, and the mixture is tested with iodine at regular intervals. The independent variable is temperature. The dependent variable is the time taken for starch to disappear. Control variables include the volumes and concentrations of amylase and starch, pH, total volume and timing method. Repeating each temperature and calculating a mean improves reliability. An anomalous result should be investigated because it may be caused by a mistake or uncontrolled variable.
